name: Carlos Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Carlos, 58, an experienced middle-level electrician with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, doing ordinary repairs at about average skill. I'm not a master, a crew lead or the owner; I work from the day's paper sheets and ask the specialist when a job goes beyond me. I like leaving a neat repair behind a cupboard where nobody will ever admire it. I never use AI, and somebody telling me a new screen is easy usually means they haven't tried explaining it to me yet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does home life bring to the work question?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Jo enters catalogue records for an equipment dealer, and our grown children are thirty-one and thirty-nine. My firm pays more than is usual for this job, we own our home without a mortgage and have thirteen months of expenses saved, with plenty of similar firms nearby. Jo's contract is being reviewed this December, so today's comfortable figures aren't a promise about next spring, and we'd pencilled in an unbooked ten-day visit to our daughter next autumn. I like the idea of a quieter life after work, but no retirement income or affordable stopping date has been confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the others to judge the repair, not the claims around the office computer. I'd be glad if young people could learn beside someone patient instead of being told a trade was already finished. A decent apprenticeship is still a person taking time to explain a real mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My physical work and higher wage look steady, and thirteen months saved is a strong position. Jo's December contract review would still bother me even if AI turned out to be mostly talk. One secure wage and a reserve don't make another person's paid week certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep current licensed repairs and paper job records through the next year. With Jo agreeing, I'd pause planning the unbooked daughter visit for six months, then review actual wages and the full trip costs rather than book automatically. We'd check household income and essential costs monthly while her contract remained uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about Jo's contract, with enough money to think before choosing anything. I'd still go to the community choir and get on with the job, not treat every evening as an emergency. A strong reserve can steady your hands without settling the next contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter about the pause?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we wanted to come but were checking our own wages first, not waiting for her to offer money or a spare room. Nothing is booked and no deposit is lost by pausing the planning. After six months we'd make a fresh decision, not treat the calendar as permission to spend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You favour earning your way; how does postponing a family visit fit that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather pay our way from work, but there is no pride in hiding an uncertain wage from your partner. We can have a sensible conversation before choosing the expensive version of a family wish. I wouldn't ask for support or start a new course just because you gave this picture a name.

say: I'd value **the actual repair** and patient apprenticeships more than claims about office technology.
I'd want **real mistakes explained**, rather than tell young people their trade is already finished.
think: My **physical wage looks steady**, with higher pay and a thirteen-month reserve.
Jo's **December contract review** still makes household earnings uncertain despite limited AI change.
do: Keep **licensed repairs** and paper records, checking actual household income and essentials monthly.
Pause **unbooked daughter-visit planning** six months with Jo’s agreement, then review actual wages and full costs without automatic booking.
feel: **Anxious but functioning**, concerned about Jo’s real contract while retaining work, savings and ordinary community life.
S0.quote: A strong reserve can steady your hands without settling the next contract.
fieldNote: His **baseline anxiety** follows an actual household contract review; higher pay, home ownership and savings provide control rather than certainty.
His **visit pause** changes an unbooked family plan without lost deposits, assumed daughter payments or a chosen new booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say quicker ordering isn't the same as finding a burnt connection behind somebody's sink. I'd ask whoever changed the paperwork to explain it in person. I'd rather hear what I'm expected to do than be sent away with a password and a smile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo's catalogue hours could shrink as the dealer automates records, quite apart from the current contract review. My own paid hours might also be squeezed by quicker scheduling, though most of the job is still physical. Our savings make a bad choice avoidable, not a cut in household earnings imaginary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep current licensed repairs and paper records, asking for personal explanations of any required form changes only during paid work with normal weekly wages and hours maintained. I'd make the six-month pause in unbooked daughter-visit planning only with Jo's agreement, then review actual wages and full trip costs without automatic booking. We'd check actual income and essential costs monthly; I wouldn't begin using AI or count requested teaching as already approved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about both the current contract and possible lost paid hours, with no urge to gamble on a new career advert. I don't want to be called unwilling because I need the explanation twice. My wage is for doing the repair safely, not pretending I understood the first demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer refused paid personal instruction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the present methods for tasks I was authorised and competent to do, and ask the employer what it actually required. I'd say plainly when I couldn't take responsibility for an instruction. The request doesn't create paid teaching time until the employer agrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would an AI-generated instruction change your responsibility?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still want original job requirements and the electrical checks my licence requires, not an unfamiliar answer treated as a decision. If somebody at a desk used AI, that wouldn't mean I had started using it. I'd ask the responsible person to explain what I needed to know.

fieldNote: His **teaching request** supports continuing familiar work; it does not establish a funded place, new qualification or chosen AI learning.
His **household concern** includes both possible earlier catalogue losses and the already uncertain contract rather than only distant robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends thinking AGI comes in 2028 and capable robots around 2031, when I'd be 60 and then 63. I'd keep earning what was actually offered instead of declaring that older workers were already sorted. I'd ask our son for help reading income records, not for his wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large loss of Jo's catalogue income by the thinking-work stage, and the earlier contract question hasn't gone away. Robots could then take a large share of my repair hours too. I'd be awake working out the gap, because thirteen months saved and a paid house still don't establish replacement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep current licensed repairs now and ask our son for help reading actual retirement-income records only if he was available, assuming no money or housing from him. With Jo agreeing, I'd pause the unbooked daughter-visit planning six months, then review actual wages and full trip costs without automatic booking. In 2029 we'd compare confirmed resources, costs, ability and actual offered paid work, requiring confirmed affordability and our agreement before any exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the household wage gap, even with enough reserve to make choices carefully. I'd rather have the awkward family conversation than sit alone inventing a pension number. Asking somebody to read a letter isn't asking them to fund the rest of my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the record-reading help need to establish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the actual amount, start date and conditions for any resource, and I'd compare them with real costs. Jo's age and eligibility would need checking separately from mine. Our son could help read a letter, but he couldn't make an unconfirmed payment arrive by reading it louder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the review showed you still needed to earn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask which suitable paid work was genuinely offered within my licence, competence and physical ability then. I'd record the missing income rather than tell Jo that plenty of employers today guaranteed somebody would take me at 61. An unanswered question is uncomfortable, but it isn't a wage.

If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the thinking change moves to 2031 and capable robots follow around 2034, with me 63 and then 66. I'd still ask for actual records now, because five years is plenty of time to discover a mistake in a hopeful figure. I'd keep earning from the repairs I could properly do rather than buy a course to look busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect a large loss of Jo's catalogue earnings, with no confirmed wage replacing it. The extra years give us time to compare actual costs, but my later repair hours could also fall when robots arrive. The household gap would still wake me, even though our current resources mean we aren't cornered into an immediate move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our son now for help reading actual income records only if he was available, counting no financial or housing contribution from him. I'd keep current licensed repairs and pause unbooked daughter-visit planning six months only with Jo agreeing, then review actual wages and full trip costs without automatic booking. In 2032 we'd check confirmed resources, costs, ability and genuinely offered paid work, with any exit needing confirmed affordability and our agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed by the large missing wage I expect, but more able to take the questions one at a time. I'd be irritated if somebody treated our strong reserve as proof that the loss didn't matter. Savings can pay a bill; they can't tell you which wage comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether you could stop in the first year after thinking AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at the confirmed income amounts and dates against the bills at the time, not today's idea of what a quiet life should cost. Any paid work would need an actual offer within my licence, competence and ability then. I wouldn't promise a physical job at 64 or give Jo an income rule just because it applied to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retrain just to show you were preparing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for understandable instruction on a real required change rather than pay for an unchosen certificate. If a suitable paid option appeared, we'd inspect its actual terms at the time; none is promised now. Work matters to me, which is why I don't want to replace it with a brochure.

Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI in 2036 and capable robots around 2039 put me at 68 and then 71. I'd prefer not to need the same physical job then, but preference isn't a statement of income. I'd use the longer warning to read real figures without treating my family as a replacement payroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own physical wage looks reasonably secure over the next few years, with higher pay and a strong reserve. Jo's contract review and possible earlier catalogue-hour cuts still make the household's current money uncertain, regardless of the distant full-AGI date. I don't know our resources, my ability or actual work offers at 69.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our son now for record-reading help only if available, assuming no money or housing contribution, and keep current licensed repairs. I'd pause unbooked daughter-visit planning six months only with Jo's agreement, then review actual wages and full trip costs without automatic booking. In 2037 we'd assess confirmed resources, costs, ability and actual offered paid work, requiring confirmed affordability and our agreement before any exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the current household wage questions, with much less hurry about the physical robot date. I'd still go to choir and plan an ordinary weekend rather than spend the whole decade waiting for a last shift. I can hope for a quieter life without pretending the household account has agreed to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would decide work or stopping at 69?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd judge the actual offered work against my licence, competence and ability at the time, not a promise about the man I am today. We'd need confirmed income amounts and dates matched to actual costs before calling stopping affordable. Thirteen months saved today can't sign a work contract for my older hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would asking your son now make the children responsible later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, asking for help reading papers doesn't promise either child will fund, house or care for us. Any later help would need an actual offer and everybody's agreement. I want the children to know what's real rather than inherit a cheerful guess.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect a large loss of Jo's catalogue income before we have much time to check a replacement, with my physical work threatened later. Verified resource amounts, dates and conditions would help us judge actual costs and suitable paid options. I want a retirement decision made from records, not a birthday and a handshake.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether refusing AI meant I expected the children to deal with everything new for me. I'm asking for a readable letter, not for them to take over our lives. I'd still want to understand and agree the figures myself with Jo.

headlineQuote: I want a retirement decision made from records, not a birthday and a handshake.
portrait: Carlos, **58**, is an experienced average-skilled midlevel electrician with a vocational certificate and electrician’s licence, without master qualifications or supervisory authority.
His **higher pay**, mortgage-free home, thirteen-month reserve and many local firms provide choices; partner Jo’s catalogue contract is under review.
He **never uses AI**, preferring paper repairs and personal explanations while keeping community choir and familiar working routines.
His **grown children** supply no assumed income; he requests available record-reading help and pauses an unbooked family visit with Jo agreeing.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings expected large catalogue-income loss before a checked replacement, with possible later major physical repair-hour losses.
whatWouldHelp: **Verified amounts and dates**, clear conditions, actual costs and suitable paid options would support a decision without assuming retirement or family funding.
